about: Proposed text_blocks.read_aloud overrides for screen and figure blocks: a short spoken description used by narration instead of the block's HTML. Drafted with model help from text_blocks.data.fields and the surrounding prose. Each is pinned to the block's sha256; if the block changes, the override no longer applies. status 'unreviewed' means no person has signed off yet.

overrides.read_aloud: Seila types a message to Jahn: Please tell me you're in Freetown and you're okay.
From Jahn: Don't worry, I am in Freetown.
And then, from Jahn: We've somehow been taking defense seriously here, and Freetown is about as far from Redshire as you can get in the United Cities, except for Silverbeach and Mabuli.
His message to Deluin: Are you okay? Please tell me where you are.
A message from Deluin: Don't worry, I am alive. Though it looks like I'm not going to be getting back to Dzego anytime soon.

Deluin again: I found a way to send messages out. Some Arctic soldier and his friend, or his AI, or something, coded up a way to embed hidden text messages inside real-time health data that he is sending back home to command. And someone else in command is relaying that signal into a weather feed, which is then going up to the satellites. He's making a whole bunch of zipcoins anonymously rebroadcasting messages for people.
Zei writes back: Wow. Are you ... in touch with this soldier?
From Deluin: I have an anonymous link.
Zei replies: Ask him how he's encoding the messages that he's putting into his health data.

Zei's message to Deluin: Or actually, on second thought, he won't answer. But tell him that randomly flipping the least-significant bits, the strategy that everyone always reaches for when they encounter this problem for the first time, is not the ideal solution. Sometimes higher-order bits are totally fine to flip, and sometimes flipping even a least-significant bit is dangerous. What you want to do is: first, train a language model on the actual distribution, so that conditional on what all the other bits are, it can give you probabilities for whether a given bit should be zero or one. Then, split the data up into buckets, using the decryption key itself to choose the buckets randomly, and require the bits in the i-th bucket to XOR to the i-th bit in the ciphertext. Within each bucket, use the model to determine which bit's probabilities are closest to fifty-fifty, meaning both values are natural for that bit to have in that context, and flip that bit to make the bucket XOR correct. So you're letting the L L M decide which bits are least significant and okay to flip, instead of just always taking the lowest-order binary digit in each number.

Another long message from Zei. If you want to go even further, it says, you can make the buckets partially overlap: the first bucket covering positions zero to one hundred ninety-nine, the second twenty to two hundred nineteen, the third forty to two hundred thirty-nine, and so on, in a pseudorandom order, with only a random half of each bucket's positions going into the XOR. Normally you flip one bit in each new stretch to make each bucket come out right in turn. But if a stretch gives you twenty bits in a row where none of them are reasonable to flip, think, a very clear picture of a night sky, then you walk back and try to find a combination of earlier bits that makes the last two buckets XOR correctly, and if that fails, walk back further, and so on.
He adds: I learned that from Den's cryptography textbooks.

From Deluin: I'll forward that to him. But I suspect that for him, first priority is going to be finding higher-bandwidth channels to hide data inside. Optimizing which bits to flip is really smart but it's maybe a two-times gain, finding a better data stream might be a thousand-times gain. Always take the dumb thousand-times gain before the super-clever two-times gain.
And then: I learned that in business school.
Zei writes: Alright, well stay safe. And let me know if there's anything that I can do, or that smart people in my network could do, to help you get out of there safely.
From Deluin: Will do. Thank you for caring about me.
A message from Deluin: Arctic soldier says thanks, it helped a lot.
